displayQuote: There is only one valid definition of a business purpose: to create a customer

meta.title: Who really said "There is only one valid definition of a business purpose: to create a customer"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Peter Drucker did write it — The Practice of Management (Harper, 1954), p. 37. His own text reads “definition of business purpose,” with no “a.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is only one valid definition of a business purpose: to create a customer'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Drucker, from The Practice of Management (Harper, 1954), p. 37 — but the circulating version adds a word he didn't write.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Drucker wrote it in The Practice of Management (New York: Harper, 1954), in the chapter “What is a business?” — Wikiquote cites it to p. 37 under its The Practice of Management (1954) heading, on a citation line that names both the Harper 1st ed. (1954) and the Routledge 2012 reprint, and Google Books full-text search returns the sentence inside its full paragraph in Drucker reprint volumes. One caveat worth knowing: his own text reads “definition of business purpose,” without the “a” the popular form inserts.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: p. 37, per Wikiquote’s sourced entry, on a citation line covering both the Harper 1st ed. (1954) and the Routledge 2012 reprint

source.excerpt: Its purpose must lie outside of the business itself. In fact, it must lie in society since business enterprise is an organ of society. There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer. Markets are not created by God, nature, or economic forces but by businessmen.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line with a page number under its heading The Practice of Management (1954). The single citation line beneath that heading covers two printings — “Harper, 1st ed. 1954 ; Routledge, 2012” — and the “p. 37” sits under the quote itself, so Wikiquote does not pin the page to one printing or the other — Wikiquote ↗.

The Internet Archive’s catalog record confirms the book: Peter F. Drucker, The practice of management, 1954, 416 pages, with a contents list that includes the chapter “What is a business?” That record catalogues the imprint as “New York: Harper & Row” — a house that did not exist until 1962, when Harper & Brothers merged with Row, Peterson & Co., so the 1954 first edition was Harper & Brothers — Internet Archive ↗.

Google Books full-text search returns the sentence in its paragraph, and settles the wording: Drucker writes “definition of business purpose,” with no article — Google Books ↗. A 2003 marketing text carries the passage on to its next move, “It is the customer who determines what a business is” — Google Books ↗.

Quote Investigator has no file on this line: a site search for “create a customer” returns nothing, and its Drucker articles cover other quotes — Quote Investigator ↗. There is no origin dispute here to adjudicate.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from a Google Books full-text snippet of a Drucker reprint volume, which returns these four sentences as one continuous passage. The 1954 Harper printing is still in copyright and its Internet Archive scan is lending-restricted, so the original page cannot be reproduced here.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: The man who put the customer outside the building
author.bio: Peter Ferdinand Drucker was born in Vienna on 19 November 1909, took a doctorate in international law at Frankfurt in 1932, emigrated to the United States in 1937, and taught at NYU from 1950 to 1971 and at Claremont Graduate University from 1971 to 2002. He died on 11 November 2005, aged 95. The Practice of Management, published in 1954, is widely considered the first book to organize the art and science of running an organization into an integrated body of knowledge — Drucker himself said it laid “the foundations of a discipline.”

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Drucker. It is his, it is properly sourced, and no rival claimant exists. What drifts is the wording — and the book it gets pinned to.

items.why: The form that circulates — and the form Wikiquote transcribes — reads “definition of a business purpose.” Drucker’s own text carries no article. A Google Books full-text search of a Drucker reprint volume returns “There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer” inside its full paragraph, while the same search of that volume for the “a” form returns nothing at all — Google Books ↗.

Drucker reused the sentence for decades, so citations scatter across his shelf. A full-text search of Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices returns it too — Google Books ↗. A citation to one of those later titles is late rather than wrong; the sentence’s first home is the 1954 book.

misattribution.truthLine: Right author, right book, one word off: Drucker wrote “There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer” in The Practice of Management (Harper, 1954), cited to p. 37 by Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, on a citation line covering both the Harper 1st ed. and the Routledge 2012 reprint.

context.heading: Why the sentence mattered
lead: The line arrives in the middle of a deliberately awkward argument. Drucker refuses to let a business define itself by what it makes or by what it earns, because — in the sentences immediately before it — “its purpose must lie outside of the business itself. In fact, it must lie in society since business enterprise is an organ of society.” Having pushed the definition all the way out into society, he then narrows it in one clause to a single person: the customer.

That inversion is why the line outlasted its decade. Wikipedia summarises Drucker’s position as holding that a company’s primary responsibility is to serve its customers, and that profit is not the primary goal but an essential condition of the company’s continued existence — Wikipedia ↗. The same article notes that The Practice of Management was later voted the third most influential management book of the twentieth century in a poll of the Fellows of the Academy of Management.
context.detailsSummary: Why we can’t show you the page
detailsBody: The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1954 Harper edition, but the book is still in copyright and the scan is lending-restricted, so its full text cannot be read or quoted from directly. The passage reproduced here comes from Google Books full-text search of later Drucker reprint volumes, which return the sentence together with the sentences on either side of it — enough to confirm both the wording and its context.

Quote Investigator has not published a file on this quote. A search of the site for “create a customer” returns nothing, and its ten Drucker articles cover other lines entirely. That absence is itself informative: QI investigates quotes whose origin is contested, and this one’s is not.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for Peter Drucker lists "There is only one valid definition of a business purpose: to create a customer" under the heading The Practice of Management (1954), citing Harper, 1st ed., p. 37 — not under Misattributed or Disputed.

Raw wikitext confirms the entry sits under the section heading "The Practice of Management (1954)" with the citation line "Peter Drucker, The Practice of Management New York,: Harper, 1st ed. 1954 ; Routledge, 2012" and the sub-bullet "p. 37".
Internet Archive catalog record: The practice of management, Peter F. Drucker (1909-2005), New York: Harper & Row, 1954, 416 pages; contents include the chapter "What is a business?".

Google Books full-text search of a Drucker reprint volume returns the snippet "...purpose must lie outside of the business itself. In fact, it must lie in society since business enterprise is an organ of society. There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer. Markets are not created by God, nature, or economic forces but by businessmen..." — the wording carries no article before "business purpose", and the same volume returns zero hits for "valid definition of a business purpose".

Google Books full-text search of Total Integrated Marketing (Hulbert, Capon and Piercy; Kogan Page, 2003) returns the snippet "...valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer. It is the customer who determines what a business is. For it is the customer, and he alone, who through being willing to pay for a good or service, converts economic...".

Google Books full-text search of Peter F. Drucker's Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices returns one hit for the phrase "valid definition of business purpose", showing Drucker reused the sentence in a later book.

Wikipedia gives Drucker's dates as born 19 November 1909, died 11 November 2005; describes him as Austrian American, a management consultant, educator and author; states that The Practice of Management was voted the third most influential management book of the 20th century in a poll of the Fellows of the Academy of Management; and summarises his view that a company's primary responsibility is to serve its customers, with profit an essential condition rather than the primary goal.

The Drucker Institute states Drucker was born in Vienna on 19 November 1909, died 11 November 2005 aged 95, earned a PhD in international law at Frankfurt in 1932, emigrated to the US in 1937, taught at NYU 1950-1971 and Claremont Graduate University 1971-2002, and that The Practice of Management (1954) is 'widely considered the first book to organize the art and science of running an organization into an integrated body of knowledge', with Drucker saying it laid 'the foundations of a discipline'.
Quote Investigator has not investigated this quote: a site search for Drucker returns ten articles, none about business purpose or creating a customer.
A Quote Investigator site search for "create a customer" returns 'Nothing Found' — no QI article covers this line.
